subject: Perimeter firewall validation and exit IP inventory
messages:
From: Camila Reyes <camila.reyes@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Porter <alex.porter@veridianhealth.org>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 18 Jun 2025 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Perimeter firewall validation and exit IP inventory

Alex —

Thanks again for taking time today. To keep the private deployment timeline on track we need two small deliverables from your side so our infra and security teams can sign off on the private endpoint:

1) A short inventory of outbound egress addresses and proxies. We only need the current public-facing NAT IP(s) or FQDNs your network uses for external services (prod/stage/dev if they differ). If you already manage an outbound proxy or transit VPC please note the proxy FQDN and whether mTLS is enforced.

2) A snippet of your firewall/export (or a CSV) that lists allowed destination IPs for third-party SaaS integrations. Your security team mentioned they could export a PDF of the rules — that works fine.

I attached a small template (egress-ip-template.csv) we use to collect: environment, current-nat-ip, proxy-fqdn, proxy-port, notes. Filling it will let our onboarding engineers generate the minimal allowlist and identify any FQDN-dependent flows that require DNS-based whitelisting rather than static IPs.

Important notes for your security team:
- Redwood’s private connector opens outbound-only connections from customer VMs to our control plane for metrics/health and to the runtime for model serving. We require a set of static egress IPs from our side for control-plane callbacks when customers opt into SaaS-managed connectivity.
- If you require inbound-only IP filtering (customer initiated), please call that out so we can propose a reverse-TLS certificate plan or mutual TLS option.

Timing: if we get the filled template + firewall export by Friday (2025-06-20) we can complete the allowlist verification and schedule a short connectivity test next week.

Thanks — short and practical is best here.

—Camila
Camila Reyes
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Camila —

Thanks, attaching what we have. Quick answers below and the export PDF is attached:

- Prod NAT IP: 34.198.71.15 (this is our primary egress NAT for platform-prod).
- Stage NAT IP: 35.192.45.77 (stage is routed through a managed proxy).
- Outbound proxy: proxy-veridian.int.veridianhealth.org:8080 (transparent, requires auth via our token gateway).
- mTLS: not enforced at the proxy layer today (we do mTLS between services internally but not for outbound proxy).

We also have a small set of partner FQDNs that we prefer to whitelist by DNS (e.g., model-registry.partner.example.com). The attached export is a firewall rules PDF that shows destination ranges and notes.

Happy to hop on a 20-min call if you need clarification.

—Alex

Alex —

Appreciate the fast follow and the export. A couple of clarifying points and a suggested validation plan: 

Summary from your reply:
- Prod NAT: 34.198.71.15
- Stage NAT: 35.192.45.77
- Proxy FQDN: proxy-veridian.int.veridianhealth.org:8080 (token auth)
- No mTLS on outbound proxy

Recommended immediate steps (we can run these with your ops folks):
1) Temporary allowlist — add Redwood control-plane IPs (we will provide a short list) to your outbound allow/egress rules for the duration of the test window only.
2) Connectivity smoke test — our engineers will initiate a short series of requests from the private runtime to a test endpoint we host; we will provide a checklist so your team can confirm packet flow in firewall logs.
3) FQDN fallback — for partner FQDNs we recommend DNS-based allowlist entries on the proxy (or allow proxy DNS resolution to those domains) because those services may change IPs.

Operational considerations we noticed in your export: a few NAT translations are behind a single public IP that handles many environments. If Veridian prefers not to broaden rules, we can also support an mTLS-based outbound connection initiated from your VPC (we'd provide certs and a short onboarding script) so you only need to permit a single service port and fingerprint. Let me know which is preferable: short-lived allowlist for quick test vs mTLS onboarding for longer-term hardened posture.

Next steps:
- Alex, can you share the firewall CSV (if possible) or confirm whether the PDF rules are exhaustive for prod/stage?
- Marissa, looping you in to confirm any approvals needed for the temporary allow window.

Thanks — I’ll attach our short-run test checklist after Marissa confirms.
